title.text: SQL for analysts: ask a database the questions you ask pandas

objects.text: How do we ask a database the same questions in the language every employer uses?

AI and Data Science Professional  |  Session 10 of 24  |  Module C: Analyse and explain
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome back. Last session you grouped and joined tables in pandas and learned to catch a merge that quietly multiplies revenue. Today we ask the same questions in SQL, the language of almost every company database. If you can use a PivotTable and a VLOOKUP, you already know the ideas.

Only the words change. And every answer will be checked against pandas, so you always know it is right.

slides.notes:
Here is what you can do by the end of today. You can write a query with the main clauses, from SELECT to LIMIT, and explain the order in which the database actually runs them. You can write an inner join and a left join, say which records each one keeps, and handle NULL without losing rows by accident.

And you can use CASE WHEN, a subquery and a CTE, and check every SQL answer against pandas. All of it runs on a SQLite copy of Lakeside Mart, inside Google Colab, with nothing to install.

slides.notes:
We have two hours. The first ten minutes bring back Session 9 and set the question for today. Then forty-five minutes of concepts with no laptops open, so you can watch the queries and their results. After a ten minute break you open the Colab notebook for a forty-five minute lab, where every SQL answer is compared with pandas.

The last ten minutes are an exit check and what you keep. The lab is where the learning sticks, so please protect that time.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  A merge ran without an error and revenue became 5.3 times too big. What happened, and what protects you?
2.  Which join type keeps every order, including walk-ins with no customer_id?
3.  What does pivot_table do that groupby alone does not?

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 9. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. A merge ran without an error and revenue became 5.3 times too big. What happened, and what protects you?

A good answer is this. Fan-out: a one-to-many merge repeated each order once per line. Check row counts before and after, and set validate.

Question two. Which join type keeps every order, including walk-ins with no customer_id?

A good answer is this. A left join from orders to customers. An inner join drops the records that have no match.

Question three. What does pivot_table do that groupby alone does not?

A good answer is this. It lays the grouped result out as a grid, with one variable down the side and one across the top, which is wide format.

If you missed one, check your notes from last session tonight. Now to today.

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: Several tables linked by keys, stored in one file. SQLite is a free database that runs inside Python.
A query is one question in SQL. A clause is one part of it, such as SELECT, WHERE or ORDER BY.
Aggregate function, GROUP BY and HAVING
COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX reduce records to one value. HAVING filters the groups that GROUP BY makes.
Combines two tables on a key. INNER keeps matches only. LEFT keeps every left record.
A missing value. A test on NULL is neither true nor false but unknown, so use IS NULL.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Relational database (SQLite). Several tables linked by keys, stored in one file. SQLite is a free database that runs inside Python.

Query and clause. A query is one question in SQL. A clause is one part of it, such as SELECT, WHERE or ORDER BY.

Aggregate function, GROUP BY and HAVING. COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX reduce records to one value. HAVING filters the groups that GROUP BY makes.

JOIN (INNER, LEFT). Combines two tables on a key. INNER keeps matches only. LEFT keeps every left record.

NULL (three-valued logic). A missing value. A test on NULL is neither true nor false but unknown, so use IS NULL.

title.text:
A relational database holds several tables
linked by keys: 9 tables in one SQLite file

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_erd_11.90x4.25_24b4d6c7.png
objects.alt: A relational database holds several tables linked by keys: 9 tables in one SQLite file

objects.text: Six of the 9 tables. PK: primary key. FK: foreign key. Three prongs: the many side.

slides.notes:
In Session 2 you saw how the Lakeside tabs link by keys. A database stores such tables together, and a relational database links them with primary keys and foreign keys. Today the database is a single file called lakeside dot db, and it holds 9 tables. This diagram shows six of them, with orders at the centre: 30,229 orders, 98,066 order lines and 2,056 returns.

The database engine is SQLite. It is free, it needs no server and no account, and it runs inside Python in Colab. Real banks use bigger engines such as PostgreSQL or SQL Server, but the SQL you learn today carries over almost unchanged. Which table would you query to count returns by reason?

objects.text: SQL keywords are written in capitals by convention. SQL ignores the difference.

slides.notes:
You already do all of this in Excel, so here is the translation. Pick columns is SELECT. Which table is FROM. AutoFilter on rows is WHERE. A PivotTable is GROUP BY with an aggregate function such as COUNT, SUM or AVG. Filtering the PivotTable totals is HAVING. Sorting is ORDER BY, and LIMIT keeps only the first few rows.

VLOOKUP is a JOIN, and a lookup column beside your whole list, where the missing ones show blank, is a left join. By convention SQL keywords are written in capitals, but the database does not mind. The pandas column shows what you did last session. Which row of this table is the one you use most in Excel?

title.text:
SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY and LIMIT:
the three largest card orders at branch B06

runs.text: SELECT names the variables to return. FROM names the table.
WHERE keeps the records that pass a test. One equals sign tests equality, and text goes in single quotes.
ORDER BY sorts. DESC means largest first. A second variable breaks ties.
LIMIT 3 keeps three records. B06 has 257 card orders in all.

slides.notes:
Here is our first query. A query is one question, written in SQL. SELECT names the variables we want back, and FROM names the table. WHERE keeps only the records that pass a test, here branch B06 and payment by card. Notice one equals sign for equality, and single quotes around text.

ORDER BY sorts the result, and DESC means largest first. A second variable, order id, breaks ties so the order is always the same. LIMIT keeps the first three. A database table has no built-in row order, so without ORDER BY the word LIMIT gives you any three rows.

Branch B06 has 257 card orders. What would change if you removed ORDER BY?

title.text:
You write SELECT first, but the database
runs FROM first and SELECT fifth

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_sql_order_11.90x4.25_5c692fb9.png
objects.alt: You write SELECT first, but the database runs FROM first and SELECT fifth

objects.text: This order is why standard SQL forbids a SELECT alias in WHERE (SQLite allows it).

slides.notes:
This picture explains most SQL errors. You write the clauses in one order, with SELECT first. The database runs them in another. First FROM chooses the table. Then WHERE keeps records. Then GROUP BY makes groups. Then HAVING keeps groups. Only fifth does SELECT pick and name the variables.

Then ORDER BY sorts, and LIMIT cuts. This is the logical order of execution. So in standard SQL WHERE cannot use a name you created in SELECT, because that name does not exist yet. Many databases, such as SQL Server, refuse it. SQLite is more relaxed and accepts it, but a portable query repeats the expression or uses a CTE.

ORDER BY can use the alias, because by then it exists. Why can HAVING use an aggregate but WHERE cannot?

title.text:
Aggregate functions reduce
many records to one value

runs.text: COUNT(customer_id) counts filled values and skips NULL: 21,058.
The difference, 9,171, is the walk-in orders.
SUM adds up revenue: UGX 1,435,614,185. MAX is the largest order: UGX 3,104,000.
AS gives a result variable a name: an alias.

slides.notes:
Aggregate functions reduce many records to one value: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX. COUNT of star counts records, and we get 30,229 orders. COUNT of a variable counts only the filled values and skips NULL, so COUNT of customer id gives 21,058. The difference of 9,171 is the walk-in orders.

You met the same idea last session as size and count in pandas. SUM gives the revenue of the sample, and MAX the largest single order, 3,104,000 shillings. The word AS gives a result a name. That name is called an alias. Which of these would you use to find the smallest order?

title.text:
GROUP BY makes one result
record per group, like a PivotTable

runs.text: GROUP BY branch_id makes one group per branch.
Each aggregate function runs once per group.
ORDER BY can use the alias revenue, because SELECT has run by then.
B01 (Kampala Central) leads with UGX 283,331,305 from 5,885 orders.

slides.notes:
GROUP BY is the PivotTable of SQL. GROUP BY branch id makes one group for each branch, and each aggregate function runs once per group, so we get one result record per branch. We sort by revenue, largest first, and keep four. ORDER BY is allowed to use the alias revenue, because by the time it runs, SELECT has already created that name.

Branch B01, Kampala Central, leads with 283,331,305 shillings from 5,885 orders. This matches the pandas groupby from last session exactly, and every query today is checked against pandas. Which variable would you group by to see revenue per payment method?

title.text:
HAVING filters the groups after
GROUP BY has made them

objects.text:
reason   n
   Damaged 683
Wrong item 473
   Expired 458

runs.text: returns has one record per returned line.
GROUP BY reason counts the returns for each reason.
HAVING COUNT(*) > 450 keeps only the groups with more than 450 returns.
The fourth reason, Changed mind, has 442 and is filtered out.

slides.notes:
HAVING filters groups. First GROUP BY reason makes one group for each return reason and counts the returns. Then HAVING keeps only the groups whose count is above 450. Three reasons pass: Damaged with 683, Wrong item with 473 and Expired with 458. The fourth reason, Changed mind, has 442, so it is filtered out.

The rule of thumb: WHERE filters records before grouping, and HAVING filters groups after. Which clause would you use to count only the returns of one product?

title.text:
An aggregate function cannot appear in WHERE,
because WHERE runs before the groups exist

runs.text: This query asks WHERE to test a count.
WHERE runs second, before GROUP BY has made any group, so there is no count yet.

slides.notes:
Here is the mistake the order of execution predicts. We asked WHERE to test COUNT of star. But WHERE runs second, before GROUP BY has made any group, so there is no count to test. SQLite stops with an error that says misuse of aggregate COUNT. The fix is to move the test to HAVING, which runs after GROUP BY.

When you meet an error message in SQL, read it and then look at the order of execution. It usually points to a clause that runs too early. What would you change in this query to make it run?

title.text:
INNER JOIN keeps matches only, and LEFT
JOIN keeps every record of the left table

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_join_types_11.90x4.25_23d8008c.png
objects.alt: INNER JOIN keeps matches only, and LEFT JOIN keeps every record of the left table

objects.text: A real excerpt joined on customer_id. Gold cells are NULL (missing).

slides.notes:
Here are the two joins you will use most, on a real excerpt. The left table has three orders, and one is a walk-in with a NULL customer id. The right table has three customers, and one of them has no order in the excerpt. An inner join keeps only the keys found in both tables, so two records.

The walk-in disappears. A left join keeps every record of the left table, so three records, and the walk-in gets NULL for the loyalty tier. Full outer and right joins exist, but SQLite added them only in version 3.39. At the time of writing Colab has an older version, 3.37, which lacks them, and you can always swap the tables of a left join.

Which join would you use to list every order with its customer tier?

title.text: INNER JOIN with aliases: revenue by region

objects.text:
region orders   revenue
 Central  14060 679043495
 Eastern   6599 319196035
Northern   2929 140789695
 Western   6641 296584960

runs.text: FROM orders AS o gives the table a short name, an alias.
ON says which variables must match: the join key.
Each branch appears once in branches, so the join is many-to-one and keeps every order.

slides.notes:
This query joins orders to branches and adds up revenue by region. Notice the aliases: orders AS o and branches AS b. They are short names that make the query easier to read. ON says which variables must match, the join key. Each branch appears once in the branches table, so this is a many-to-one join and every order finds exactly one branch.

The row count does not change. Central leads with 679,043,495 shillings from 14,060 orders. The same fan-out danger from last session applies in SQL: if the right table repeated the key, revenue would be inflated. Which table would you join to get revenue by product category?

title.text:
LEFT JOIN keeps the walk-in
orders, and their loyalty tier is NULL

objects.text:
loyalty_tier orders
       Basic  13075
        NULL   9171
      Silver   5801
        Gold   2182

runs.text: Every order is kept, so the counts add up to all orders.
The NULL group holds the 9,171 walk-in orders: no customer, so no match.
An INNER JOIN to customers would return 21,058 rows, which is 9,171 fewer than the 30,229 orders.
GROUP BY puts all NULL values into one group.

slides.notes:
Here is the left join in action. We join orders to customers and count orders by loyalty tier. Every order is kept, so the counts add up to 30,229. The group with a NULL tier holds 9,171 orders: these are the walk-ins, who have no customer record to match.

An inner join would have returned only 21,058 rows, and the report would silently lose those sales. Notice that GROUP BY puts all the NULL values together into one group. Is a walk-in order a problem to fix, or a fact to report?

title.text:
A test on NULL is neither true nor
false, so WHERE drops the record

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_three_valued_7.70x4.80_0ced6bb2.png
objects.alt: A test on NULL is neither true nor false, so WHERE drops the record

objects.text: Three-valued logic: a test can be TRUE, FALSE or UNKNOWN.

runs.text: NULL means unknown, so any comparison with it is UNKNOWN.
To find NULL, write IS NULL. To keep it in a test, add OR customer_id IS NULL.

slides.notes:
Now NULL, the source of most silent SQL mistakes. NULL means unknown. If you ask whether an unknown value is different from C0495, the answer is unknown: it is neither true nor false. SQL has three values: TRUE, FALSE and UNKNOWN. WHERE keeps only the records where the test is TRUE.

So a test for customer id not equal to C0495 keeps 21,050 orders, finds 8 that equal C0495, and quietly drops the 9,171 walk-ins, which are UNKNOWN. The three numbers add up to every order. To test for NULL write IS NULL, never equals NULL. What would the test return for a walk-in if you wrote customer id equals NULL?

title.text:
IS NULL finds the missing values
that an equals test cannot see

runs.text: SUM(customer_id <> 'C0495') adds up the TRUE results: 1 for TRUE, nothing for UNKNOWN.
SUM(customer_id = 'C0495') adds up the orders of that customer.
SUM(customer_id IS NULL) counts the NULL values.
The three add up to 30,229, every order.

slides.notes:
This query counts the three outcomes of the test. In SQLite a TRUE result counts as one, so a sum of a test counts the records that pass. The first column, not equal to C0495, gives 21,050. The second, equal to C0495, gives 8. The third, IS NULL, gives 9,171.

Together they make 30,229, every order in the file. If you had trusted the not equal test alone, you would have lost the walk-ins. A good habit: whenever a variable can be NULL, count the NULL values first. Which variable in the returns table could have NULL values?

title.text:
CASE WHEN makes a new
categorical variable inside a query

runs.text: CASE tests the conditions from top to bottom and returns the first match.
It is the IF function of SQL. The pandas twin is pd.cut with right=False.
The bands are in UGX: Small under 20,000, Medium under 100,000, Large the rest.
SQLite lets GROUP BY use the alias band. Other databases need the CASE expression repeated.

slides.notes:
CASE WHEN is the IF of SQL. It tests the conditions from top to bottom and returns the value of the first one that is true. ELSE catches everything left. Here we turn the order value into a band: Small under twenty thousand shillings, Medium under a hundred thousand, and Large for the rest.

Then GROUP BY band counts the orders in each: 14,486 Medium, 13,529 Small and 2,214 Large. In pandas the same job is done with pd.cut with right equals False, so that an order of exactly 20,000 falls in Medium as it does in SQL, and then the counts agree.

SQLite lets GROUP BY use the alias band. Other databases need the CASE expression written again. Why is the order of the WHEN lines important?

title.text:
A subquery is a query inside brackets
that supplies a value to another query

runs.text: The inner query computes the average unit price: UGX 11,523.
The outer query counts the products priced above it.

slides.notes:
A subquery is a query inside brackets that provides a value to another query. The inner query computes the average unit price of all products, about 11,523 shillings. The outer query then counts the products priced above that average. The answer is 20 out of 150. In Excel you would put the average in a helper cell and compare with it.

The subquery is that helper cell, hidden inside the query. In pandas it is a comparison with the mean. How could you count the products below average?

title.text:
A CTE (WITH) names a subquery
first, so the main query reads in order

runs.text: WITH names a temporary result: a common table expression (CTE).
by_branch has one record per branch.
The main query then reads it like a table.
It finds 8 branches and a best revenue of UGX 283,331,305.

slides.notes:
A common table expression, or CTE, starts with the word WITH. It gives a name to a subquery, here by branch, which has one record per branch. The main query below then reads it like an ordinary table. We count the branches, 8, and find the best revenue, 283,331,305 shillings.

A CTE does the same job as a subquery, but it reads from top to bottom, which is easier when a query has several steps. Analysts at banks and telecoms use CTEs all the time. Which is easier for you to read, a subquery or a CTE?

title.text:
sqlite3 and pandas.read_sql: run SQL
in Colab and compare with pandas

runs.text: read_sql runs a SQL query and returns a DataFrame.
The pandas filter gives the same answer: 3,562 orders at branch B04.
a == b prints True when SQL and pandas agree.

slides.notes:
This is the habit for the whole lab. Python talks to SQLite with the sqlite3 library. Connect opens the database file, and pandas read underscore sql runs a query and hands back a DataFrame. The SQL query counts the orders at branch B04, and the pandas filter on the orders file counts the same thing.

Both give 3,562, and the last print says True. When two independent methods agree, you can trust the number. When they disagree, one of them is wrong, and finding out which teaches you the most. What would you compare next?

Here is a cheat sheet that you will build yourself in the lab. Each row is a question we answered today, with the SQL and the pandas version. Revenue by branch is GROUP BY with SUM, or groupby and sum. Groups above a size use HAVING, or value counts and a filter.

Adding the region is a join, or a merge. Bands are CASE WHEN, or pd.cut with right equals False. Walk-ins are IS NULL, or isna. And products above the average price use a subquery, or a comparison with the mean. The lab asks you to reproduce three SQL answers in pandas and compare them.

Which direction is easier for you, SQL or pandas?

title.text:
Your employer's database may not be
SQLite: four places where the dialect differs

rows.text: PostgreSQL: DATE_TRUNC or TO_CHAR. SQL Server: FORMAT or DATEFROMPARTS. MySQL: DATE_FORMAT.
SQL Server and Access: SELECT TOP 3. Oracle: FETCH FIRST 3 ROWS ONLY.
The SQL standard and many databases refuse it. Repeat the expression or use a CTE.
Available in PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Oracle and MySQL (full outer join in MySQL needs a workaround).

title.text: Five likely mistakes in the lab and how to fix them

rows.text: The variable is in another table, or misspelt.
Check the table with SELECT * FROM table LIMIT 3.
A WHERE test returns fewer records than expected
NULL values make the test UNKNOWN.
Count IS NULL first, and add OR variable IS NULL if needed.
Revenue much bigger after a JOIN
The right table repeats the key: fan-out.
Count the rows before and after. Summarise the right table first.
The result order changes between runs
No ORDER BY, so the order is not defined.
Add ORDER BY, with a second variable to break ties.

Five messages and symptoms you may meet. No such column means the variable is in another table or misspelt, so look at the first rows of the table. Misuse of aggregate means you put an aggregate in WHERE, so move it to HAVING. A test that returns fewer records than you expected is usually NULL, so count the NULL values first.

Revenue much bigger after a join is fan-out, so count the rows before and after. And a result that changes order between runs has no ORDER BY. Read the message first. It usually tells you the answer.

title.text:
Exit check: three questions, then
compare with the short answers

rows.text: Which clause runs first in a SQL query, and which runs fifth?
FROM runs first. SELECT runs fifth, after WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING. That is why the SQL standard does not let WHERE use an alias made in SELECT. SQLite allows it, many databases do not.
An INNER JOIN of orders to customers returns 21,058 rows and a LEFT JOIN returns 30,229. Why?
9,171 orders have a NULL customer_id, so they have no match. The inner join drops them and the left join keeps them.
Why does WHERE customer_id <> 'C0495' not return the walk-in orders?
A comparison with NULL is UNKNOWN, and WHERE keeps only TRUE. Add OR customer_id IS NULL.
